title: Majority Element
description: Brute force to optimized: counting every candidate versus a frequency map versus Boyer-Moore voting.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element, the value that appears more than n divided by 2 times. It is guaranteed that a majority element always exists in the array.

blocks.text: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element, the value that appears more than n divided by 2 times. It is guaranteed that a majority element always exists in the array.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Landslide Election Result
blocks.text: Like counting votes where one candidate is guaranteed to have won more than half of all votes cast. Even without a full formal tally, tracking a single leading candidate and a running lead count is enough to identify the winner.

blocks.caption: One value appears in more than half of the array

blocks.text: With a single element, that element trivially appears more than half the time, so the answer is 1.
It is worth asking what the "a majority element is guaranteed to exist" constraint actually buys beyond just simplifying the problem statement.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Counting each distinct value exactly once, with a hash map, already removes the brute force's repeated recounting, the same frequency counting idea used elsewhere in this sheet.

Observation 2: This problem carries a stronger guarantee than most: the majority element does not just appear most often, it appears more than every other value COMBINED, since it exceeds n divided by 2.

Observation 3: That guarantee turns the array into a cancellation game, if every occurrence of the majority element is paired off against a different value and both cancel, there still cannot be enough non-majority values left to cancel every majority occurrence.

Observation 4: Testing nums equal to [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2] confirms it, even though the running candidate briefly switches to 1 partway through, the true majority value 2 always ends up the one left standing once every value has taken its turn either adding to or cancelling the running count.

Recognizing that "more than half" specifically means "outnumbers everything else combined" is what unlocks the cancellation trick, rather than treating the guarantee as just a convenience that avoids an edge case.
For every distinct value in the array, count how many times it occurs by scanning the whole array, and return the value whose count exceeds half the array length.

items: For every index i, treat nums[i] as a candidate.
Count how many times this candidate appears across the whole array.
If that count is more than n divided by 2, return the candidate.

codes.python:
def majority_element(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    for i in range(n):                                      # try every element as a candidate
        candidate = nums[i]
        count = 0
        for num in nums:                                       # count how often it actually appears
            if num == candidate:
                count += 1
        if count > n // 2:
            return candidate
    return -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
    print(majority_element(nums))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every index is tried as a candidate, even though many indices share the same value and end up recomputing an identical count.
Each candidate's count is computed by scanning the entire array from scratch, with no memory carried over between candidates.
The function returns as soon as a count exceeds n divided by 2, relying on the guarantee that exactly one such value exists.

blocks.text: Since a majority element is guaranteed to exist, checking every candidate's true count will always find it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), a full rescan for every candidate.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.
Limitation: the same counts get recomputed repeatedly whenever a value repeats as a candidate, instead of being counted just once per distinct value.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing every candidate's count works but is wasteful: a value that repeats many times as a candidate has its full count recomputed from scratch every single time it appears.

What a hash map fixes directly: tallying every value's frequency in a single pass, so each distinct value is counted exactly once instead of once per occurrence.

Can the counting be avoided entirely: yes, but only because of the specific "more than half" guarantee this problem provides, which is stronger than a typical frequency question.

What does that guarantee actually unlock: a cancellation game, where a running candidate and count can track the majority value without ever recording a full frequency table.

The core idea: build a frequency map first as the general purpose fix, then recognize the guaranteed-majority constraint allows an even leaner running candidate and count instead.

Count every value exactly once using a hash map from value to frequency, built in a single pass. Once every count is known, the value whose count exceeds half the array length is the majority element.
Build a frequency map in one pass, then scan it for the value exceeding half the array length.

blocks.caption: Optimized: count every value once, then find the one exceeding half the array length

blocks.text: This works because the frequency map accumulates the exact true count of every distinct value across a single pass, and since a majority element is guaranteed to exist, scanning the finished map for the one count exceeding n divided by 2 is guaranteed to find it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to count, one pass over the distinct values.
Space: O(n), for the frequency map in the worst case.

Because the majority element is guaranteed to occur more than n divided by 2 times, it can outlast every other value in a simple cancellation game: keep one running candidate and a count. On each new value, if the count is 0, adopt this value as the new candidate. If the value matches the candidate, increment the count, otherwise decrement it. Every non majority value can cancel out at most as many majority votes as its own occurrences allow, so the majority element is guaranteed to be the candidate left standing at the end.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: a single running candidate survives every cancellation

items: Whenever the running count reaches 0, the current value is adopted as the new candidate, restarting the cancellation game from that point onward.
Every value that matches the current candidate increments the count, while every mismatch decrements it, exactly mirroring votes cast for versus against the current candidate.

Since the true majority element occurs more than every other value combined, it is mathematically guaranteed to survive as the final candidate, regardless of how the count rises and falls along the way.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per element.
Space: O(1), only the candidate and count are kept, no frequency map needed.

blocks.text: This problem's further round, Boyer-Moore voting, is a specific trick that only works because a true majority element is guaranteed to exist. Without that guarantee, the algorithm would still return some value, but it would need a second pass to verify that value actually occurs more than half the time.

items: Applying Boyer-Moore voting when a majority element is not guaranteed to exist, without adding a verification pass afterward.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra space", think: Boyer-Moore voting, a running candidate and count, relying on the guaranteed majority.
If the interviewer says "what if a majority is not guaranteed", think: Boyer-Moore voting still finds a candidate, but a second verification pass is now required.
If the interviewer says "why does the cancellation trick actually work", think: the majority element outnumbers every other value combined, so it can never be fully cancelled away.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (Boyer-Moore voting): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: frequency counting, further reduced to the Boyer-Moore voting trick, a cancellation game that exploits the guarantee that a true majority exists.

Core Idea: since the majority element outnumbers every other value combined, a single running candidate and count, adopting a new candidate whenever the count hits zero, is guaranteed to converge on the true majority element.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the frequency map version, O(1) for Boyer-Moore voting.
Most Important Observation: "more than half" is a much stronger guarantee than "most common", and that extra strength is exactly what makes a pure cancellation trick correct.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write a correct frequency map version; deriving and explaining why Boyer-Moore voting is correct is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: adopt a new candidate when the count hits zero, add on a match, subtract on a mismatch.
